one_liner: Three header-only lower_bound variants (branchless cmov, cmov+prefetch, Eytzinger layout); 5.8x std::lower_bound in L1, 1.9x from DRAM on ints.
what_it_does: include/fastcpp/algo/binary_search.hpp in the developer source/fastcpp repo offers three ways to search a contiguous sorted array. lower_bound_branchless and lower_bound_prefetch take (const T* base, size_t n, const T& key, Compare = std::less<>) and return a const T* to the element std::lower_bound would find; the tests check this against std::lower_bound for every key over a 5,000-int array. build_eytzinger plus lower_bound_eytzinger copy the sorted data into an (n+1)-slot breadth-first array. The search then returns an Eytzinger tree index (0 means end), which you read back as tree[index]; it is not a position in the sorted array.
how_it_is_fast: Branchless binary search: the step is spelled `base += size_t(less(base[half-1], key)) * half`, which gcc 13 compiles to cmovge. That removes the ~log2(n) unpredictable branches that std::lower_bound mispredicts. The prefetch variant also __builtin_prefetch-es both candidate next probes, which restores the free prefetching that a branchy search gets from speculatively loading wrong-path elements; that is why it still wins once the array misses to DRAM. The Eytzinger layout (Khuong & Morin, 'Array layouts for comparison-based searching') stores the implicit search tree breadth-first so the top levels share cache lines, prefetches tree[index*16] (the node's descendants four levels down) and recovers the answer from the final index's trailing ones with std::countr_one.
when_to_use: Hot lower_bound calls on a read-only sorted array of small, cheaply compared keys that fits in cache: plain branchless measured 11.6 ns vs 67.4 ns per query on 4,096 ints (16 KiB).

Sorted arrays larger than cache where you must keep sorted order and get a position back: use lower_bound_prefetch, the only variant the repo records as a stable win there (1.91x in the published row; the header comment says 'a stable 1.6x').

Build-once, search-many lookup tables larger than cache where you can give up sorted order: on the same 4.2M-int array the Eytzinger layout measured 80.1 ns against 317.1 ns for branchless, about 5.3x std::lower_bound's 427.7 ns in that run.
Batches of independent lookups (the benchmark's shape: 20,000 unrelated random keys per pass) built with GCC on x86-64, the only toolchain and ISA the numbers cover.
when_not_to_use: Memory-bound searches with the plain branchless function: the repo records it at 0.72x-1.49x of std::lower_bound on the 16 MiB array across five runs, so it can lose.
Cache-resident arrays with the prefetch variant: there it was slower than plain branchless (14.9 vs 11.6 ns), because the wasted prefetches still use load slots.

Exact-match lookups where ordering doesn't matter: on a 92-keyword set the same repo measured a sorted array plus binary search at 69.7 ns, its flat_hash_map at 8.9 ns and its perfect hash table at 3.3 ns.

Data that changes between searches, or callers who need an iterator or rank from the Eytzinger search: the layout leaves the array unsorted, must be rebuilt after any change, and returns a tree index.

Other compilers, clang, MSVC or non-int keys without re-measuring: the header warns the cmov codegen 'is not stable across compilers or versions', FASTCPP_PREFETCH_READ is a no-op outside GCC/Clang, and only gcc 13.3 with libstdc++ on one Xeon VM was benchmarked.

integration.dependencies: none beyond fastcpp/core/macros.hpp (for FASTCPP_ALWAYS_INLINE and FASTCPP_PREFETCH_READ) and <bit>, <cstddef>, <functional>, <iterator>. The two files total 268 lines and can be copied out if you have access to the private repo.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 for this header (std::countr_one from <bit>). The repo itself builds as C++23 and lists gcc 13+, clang 17+ or MSVC 19.35+. Published numbers exist only for gcc 13.3.0.
integration.platforms: Portable C++. Explicit prefetch exists only on GCC/Clang (__builtin_prefetch) and is a no-op on MSVC. Benchmarked only on an x86-64 Intel Xeon (AVX2) cloud VM. The CI matrix includes macOS clang, but at HEAD that job fails to compile an unrelated xsimd benchmark, so the search tests don't run there.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. All three searches are noexcept pure reads of a caller-owned const array with no internal state, so concurrent searches of an unchanging array share nothing mutable.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — lower_bound_branchless and lower_bound_prefetch return the same element as std::lower_bound (tested per key), but they take a raw pointer plus count instead of an iterator pair and return const T*, so they work only on contiguous storage. The Eytzinger search needs a separately built array and returns a tree index, not a position.

gotchas: The win depends on how the step is spelled. `base = less(...) ? base + half : base` compiles to a branch (jle) on gcc 13 and is no faster than std::lower_bound; only the multiply-by-bool form emits cmov. If you edit, port or upgrade the compiler, check the disassembly.
Every function is noexcept whatever Compare or T is, so a throwing comparator (or a throwing copy-assignment inside build_eytzinger) calls std::terminate.

lower_bound_eytzinger prefetches &tree[index * 16], which for the deeper levels points far past the end of the array. The prefetch doesn't fault, but the pointer arithmetic is out of bounds. The distance is fixed at 16 elements whatever sizeof(T) is (one 64-byte line only for 4-byte keys), and build_eytzinger doesn't cache-line-align its output. Only int was benchmarked.

The published ns are per-query averages over the same 20,000 independent keys replayed every pass, so the CPU can overlap consecutive searches; the latency of a single dependent lookup is not measured. These rows also come from the -O2 run (2026-09-02-core) and weren't re-measured after the repo moved its benchmarks to -O3 on 2026-09-03.
verified_claims_summary: The repo's own bench_doing_less (20,000 random-key queries per pass, minimum of 7 samples) compares against libstdc++ std::lower_bound on gcc 13.3.0 -O2 -march=native on a shared 4-core Intel Xeon 2.1 GHz VM: branchless takes 11.6 vs 67.4 ns per query on 4,096 ints (5.83x), and the prefetch variant 224.0 vs 427.7 ns on 4,194,304 ints (1.91x). On that same 4.2M array the Eytzinger layout took 80.1 ns, 3.96x faster than the branchless search it was timed next to. That puts it about 5.3x ahead of std::lower_bound, but the 5.3x comes from comparing two tables in the same run, not from one direct measurement.
status_note: The repo is private (0 stars; only readable with access) and saw a single 13-commit burst on 2026-09-02..04, with the header unchanged since the first commit; the code is MIT and 268 lines to vendor, but all 21 CI runs failed — at HEAD the search tests pass in the asan+ubsan and gcc-native jobs, and the failures are in unrelated targets.
